notes.h: Minerals: what they are and how they are classed
notes.b: Minerals are the part of food that is not made by living things at all. The body needs them in small amounts to build structures, run processes and make enzymes and hormones.
points: Minerals are inorganic elements (not made by living things) that the body cannot make, so they must be obtained from food. They build body structures, regulate body processes and form parts of enzymes and hormones.
Major (macro) minerals are needed in larger amounts, above 100 mg a day. They are calcium, phosphorus, potassium, sodium, chloride, magnesium and sulphur.

Minerals are not destroyed by cooking, because they are elements. They can, however, be lost into cooking water and in the trimming of food. For example, boiling vegetables in a lot of water washes minerals out.
The RDA (recommended daily amount) is the daily intake that meets the needs of almost everyone in a group. It differs with age, sex, pregnancy and breastfeeding, so some groups need more than others.

Phosphorus works with calcium to harden bones and teeth and forms part of ATP (the cell's energy carrier) and cell membranes. Sources are milk, cheese, meat, fish, eggs, wholegrains and nuts, and deficiency is rare.
notes.tip: Examiners accept calcium or phosphorus lack as the cause of osteomalacia, so know phosphorus as calcium's partner in bone.

notes.b: Calcium is the most important mineral for the skeleton, but it also keeps blood, muscles and nerves working. Because bone is built in childhood and lost in later life, some groups need more of it.
points: Milk, cheese and yoghurt are the richest dietary sources of calcium. This is why dairy foods matter for bone health.

Canned sardines and canned salmon eaten with their bones, green leafy vegetables such as kale, broccoli and cabbage, calcium-set tofu, fortified plant milks and fortified breakfast cereals are further sources.
Calcium works with phosphorus to form the mineral salts that give bones and teeth their hardness. This is why a diet low in calcium leaves bones weak.
Calcium is needed for blood clotting, normal muscle contraction (including the heartbeat) and nerve impulse transmission. It also activates some enzymes and helps regulate blood pressure.
Rickets in children (soft, bent bones and poor teeth) and osteomalacia in adults result from too little calcium, phosphorus or vitamin D.

Osteoporosis, which develops over years, makes bones thin, porous, brittle and prone to fracture, with loss of height and a stooped back. Other effects of low calcium are tooth decay, slow clotting, and muscle cramps (tetany) and poor nerve function.
Osteoporosis risk is raised by low calcium and vitamin D intake, lack of weight-bearing exercise, smoking, alcohol, the fall in oestrogen after menopause and family history.

Need is highest when bone is being built (childhood, teenage years, pregnancy, breastfeeding) and when it is lost (women after menopause). Bone density peaks in the late teens and twenties, so teenage intake matters.
notes.tip: Do not offer spinach or rhubarb as calcium sources: their calcium is bound by oxalate and poorly absorbed. Osteoporosis (thin, porous bone) is a different condition from osteomalacia and rickets (soft bone).

notes.b: Iron is needed to carry oxygen, so a shortage leaves the whole body short of energy. It comes in two forms, and the form decides how easily the body absorbs it.
points: Haem iron comes from animal foods and is absorbed easily. Sources are red meat, liver and offal, kidney, black pudding, poultry and oily fish.

Non-haem iron comes from plant foods and eggs and is absorbed less easily. Sources are eggs, wholegrain and fortified cereals, wholemeal bread, pulses, dark green leafy vegetables, dried apricots and other dried fruit, nuts and seeds.
Iron is an essential part of haemoglobin, the red protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs around the body to all cells.

Iron is part of myoglobin, which stores oxygen in muscle cells, and part of enzymes that release energy from food. It also supports immunity and concentration. This is why a shortage leaves people tired.

Iron deficiency causes anaemia (too few red blood cells or too little haemoglobin). Effects are tiredness, pale skin, breathlessness, dizziness, irritability, poor concentration, feeling cold and reduced resistance to infection.
Causes of iron deficiency are a diet low in iron or poor in vitamin C, blood loss (menstruation, ulcers, operations), high needs in growth spurts, pregnancy and infancy, and poor absorption.

Corrective measures are eating more iron-rich foods together with vitamin C, avoiding tea with meals, and taking an iron supplement on medical advice. This is because vitamin C improves absorption and tea blocks it.

Groups at risk are teenage girls, menstruating and pregnant women, infants and toddlers, people with heavy blood loss, and vegetarians and vegans, who eat only non-haem iron. Children are at risk because of fast growth and low-iron foods. For example, vegetarians miss out on the more easily absorbed haem form.
notes.tip: Split iron sources into haem and non-haem when asked. Anaemia means too little haemoglobin and is not a synonym for iron deficiency, which is only its commonest cause: lack of B12 or folate can also cause it.

notes.h: Trace minerals needed in the diet (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Trace minerals are needed in only tiny amounts, yet the body cannot do without them. Each has a job that no other mineral can do.
points: Trace (micro) minerals are needed in only tiny amounts, measured in milligrams or micrograms a day, and the diet must supply them. They are tiny in amount yet essential. For example, zinc and iodine are needed in milligrams or micrograms.
The trace minerals are iron, zinc, iodine, fluoride, copper, selenium, manganese, chromium and cobalt. Iron is a trace mineral by the amount needed, but it is studied in detail at Ordinary Level.
Iron, zinc and iodine each play a specific role in the body that the other minerals cannot replace. Zinc and iodine are set out in the blocks that follow.
notes.tip: If asked to name trace minerals, give at least four from the list above.

notes.b: Zinc is a trace mineral that works inside enzymes, so it affects growth, healing and defence against infection.
points: Zinc sources include oysters and other shellfish, red meat, poultry, liver, dairy products, eggs, wholegrain cereals, pulses, nuts and seeds.
Zinc is a component of many enzymes and supports growth and cell division, which is why a shortage slows growth in children.
Zinc supports wound healing and a healthy immune system. This is because new cells must be made to repair the wound.
Zinc contributes to a normal sense of taste and smell, and to healthy skin and hair and reproductive health.
Deficiency causes poor growth, delayed wound healing, dry flaky skin and rashes, loss of taste and appetite, reduced immunity and hair loss.
notes.tip: In matching questions, dry flaky skin points to zinc deficiency.

notes.b: Iodine is needed to make a hormone that sets the body's pace. Without it the thyroid gland cannot do its job.
points: Iodine sources include sea fish and shellfish, seaweed, milk and dairy products and eggs. Iodised salt also exists as a source.
Iodine is part of thyroxine, the hormone from the thyroid gland that controls the rate of metabolism (and growth and brain development).
Deficiency causes goitre, a swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck as it works harder to make more thyroxine. This is because the gland enlarges as it works harder.
Iodine deficiency causes tiredness and sluggishness (lethargy) and weight gain in adults. It causes delayed mental and physical development in children, and in babies of deficient mothers.
notes.tip: Goitre is the iodine deficiency disease. Do not confuse it with cretinism or with an overactive thyroid.

notes.b: Potassium and sodium work as a pair, one inside cells and one outside, to keep fluid, nerves and muscles balanced.
points: Potassium sources include bananas, potatoes eaten in their skins, tomatoes, dried fruit, orange juice, pulses, green and leafy vegetables, milk, meat, fish and nuts.
Potassium is the main positive ion (electrolyte) inside cells and, with sodium, helps regulate fluid balance in and around cells.
Potassium is needed to transmit nerve impulses and for muscle contraction, including the heartbeat. This is why a shortage causes cramps.
Potassium works with sodium to regulate blood pressure, and a high potassium intake helps lower it.
Deficiency (hypokalaemia) causes muscle weakness, cramps, an irregular heartbeat and tiredness. It is usually caused by severe vomiting, diarrhoea or some medicines rather than by normal diets.
notes.tip: If asked for one main function of potassium, give nerve impulses, muscle contraction or fluid balance.

notes.b: Sodium is essential, and the problem in Ireland is eating too much of it, not too little. Most of it comes from salt, which is sodium chloride.
points: Sodium is mainly consumed as salt. Table salt, cured and smoked meats and fish such as bacon and ham, cheese, bread, crisps and snack foods, processed and ready meals, sauces, stock cubes and canned foods supply most of it.
Fresh, unprocessed foods contain only small amounts of naturally occurring sodium. This is why processed foods, such as bacon and ready meals, are the main source.
Sodium is the main positive ion (electrolyte) outside cells and, with potassium, regulates fluid balance and blood volume.
Sodium is needed to transmit nerve impulses, for muscle contraction and for enzyme function. It helps the small intestine absorb glucose and some amino acids. This is why a shortage causes cramps.

Excess sodium raises blood pressure (hypertension), which increases the risk of stroke, heart disease and kidney problems. Most people in Ireland eat more salt than advised, mostly from processed foods.
To cut salt, cook from fresh food, do not add salt at the table, read labels (salt is on the nutrition declaration) and choose low-salt products.

The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) began a voluntary Salt Reduction Programme in 2003 to cut salt in processed food. Later reformulation work continues under the FSAI-Healthy Ireland Food Reformulation Task Force.
Deficiency is uncommon but causes muscle cramps, headache, nausea and confusion. It can follow heavy sweating, vomiting or diarrhoea.
notes.tip: Salt and sodium are not the same: salt is sodium chloride. Do not call sodium bad, since the body needs it and the harm comes from excess. For a sodium question give functions such as fluid balance and nerve impulses, plus sources such as bacon, cheese and crisps.

keyTerms.definition: A mineral needed by the body in amounts above 100 mg a day, such as calcium, phosphorus, potassium or sodium.
A mineral needed by the body in very small amounts, such as iron, zinc or iodine.
The iron-containing protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues.
The iron-containing protein in muscle cells that stores oxygen for muscle use.
The thyroid hormone, containing iodine, that controls the rate of metabolism.
An enlargement of the thyroid gland, usually caused by a lack of iodine.
A mineral that carries an electrical charge in body fluids, such as sodium or potassium, and helps regulate fluid balance.
A condition in which bone density falls, making bones thin, brittle and prone to fracture.
A condition in which the blood has too few healthy red blood cells or too little haemoglobin to carry enough oxygen.
A condition in adults in which bones become soft and painful because of a lack of calcium, phosphorus or vitamin D.

questions.prompt: Give two functions of calcium in the body and name one food that supplies it.
questions.model: Any two of: formation of strong bones and teeth; blood clotting; normal muscle contraction, including the heartbeat; nerve impulse transmission. Any one calcium food, such as milk, cheese, yoghurt, canned sardines or leafy greens. One mark for each correct function and one for the food.

questions.prompt: Discuss the importance of iron and calcium in the diet, including their sources, functions and the effects of a deficiency of each.
questions.model: Iron: haem iron from red meat, liver, offal, poultry and fish; non-haem iron from eggs, wholegrain cereals, pulses, dark green vegetables, dried fruit, nuts and seeds. Functions: forms haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in red blood cells; forms myoglobin in muscles; part of enzymes that release energy from food. Deficiency: iron-deficiency anaemia with tiredness, pale skin, breathlessness and poor concentration. Calcium: milk, cheese, yoghurt, canned sardines and salmon with bones, leafy greens. Functions: forms strong bones and teeth; needed for blood clotting, muscle contraction and nerve impulses. Deficiency: rickets in children, osteomalacia and osteoporosis in adults, with bones that soften, break easily or lose density. Vitamin D aids calcium absorption and vitamin C aids non-haem iron absorption.
